LLM auditresponse for paradox-launcher:
<security_assessment>
<decision>UNSAFE</decision>
<details>
The script copies files from <code>/opt/paradox-launcher/</code> to a user-writable directory <code>${HOME}/.paradox-launcher</code> and then executes a script from that directory. This creates a privilege escalation and persistence risk if an attacker has write access to <code>/opt/paradox-launcher</code> or the home directory. More critically, the use of <code>cp /opt/paradox-launcher/* "$DIR" -R</code> without validation allows arbitrary code in the source directory to be copied and potentially executed. If the source directory is writable by an untrusted user or process, this could lead to remote code execution.

The most severe issue is that the script executes <code>bootstrapper.sh</code> from user-writable <code>$DIR</code> without verifying its origin or integrity. An attacker could replace or modify this script after the initial copy, leading to arbitrary code execution on subsequent runs. This pattern is commonly exploited in supply chain attacks where a benign script is later hijacked via file replacement.
</details>
<evidence>
cp /opt/paradox-launcher/* "$DIR" -R
chmod +x "$DIR"/data/bootstrapper/bootstrapper.sh
"$DIR"/data/bootstrapper/bootstrapper.sh
</evidence>
<summary>
Executes unverified script from user-writable directory</summary>
</security_assessment>

The concern about trust in the source directory is a system configuration issue (i.e., ensuring /opt/paradox-launcher is properly secured), not an inherent flaw or malicious act in the AUR packaging.

LLM auditresponse for paradox-launcher:
 <security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This is a standard per-user launcher wrapper. It creates `~/.paradox-launcher` on first use, copies the installed application files from `/opt/paradox-launcher/` into it, makes the upstream bootstrapper executable, and runs it. There are no network downloads, no encoded commands, no `eval`, no `curl`/`wget` piping, and no writes outside the application's own per-user directory. Running the application's bootstrapper from the user-writable copy is expected behavior for launchers that need write access or self-update capabilities; it is not injected malicious code.

The only mild consideration is that the script executes `~/.paradox-launcher/data/bootstrapper/bootstrapper.sh` from the user's home directory. On a single-user system this is no different from running the installed launcher. It could only become a local code-execution hazard if an attacker can pre-create or modify `~/.paradox-launcher`, which requires either same-user access (already equivalent to code execution) or a misconfigured/world-writable home directory. This is a packaging/hygiene nuance, not evidence of a supply-chain attack, so the file is marked SAFE.
</details>
<evidence>
